Abstract This study aims to present a bibliometric analysis in the domain of economic policy uncertainty (EPU) by consolidating existing studies in the area from 2006-2022. The research unravels the knowledge structure of the field by examining intellectual and conceptual aspects. A total of 2025 papers were found from the initial search of the Scopus database, and 1055 were finalized after the screening. To understand the characteristics, hot topics and emerging themes in the field of EPUs, various tools, such as cocitation analysis, bibliographic coupling, alluvial maps, and thematic analysis, that were analyzed via VOS viewer software and Biblioshiny R were used. The most important themes that emerged from the cocitation analysis and bibliographic coupling included stock market volatility, oil price shocks, spillover effects and fluctuations. The thematic analysis highlighted the emerging themes of consumption behavior, disasters, environmental economics, carbon, the energy market and alternative energy and volatility forecasting. This study utilizes only the Scopus database and includes only published works in the field in English. The study presents an overview of the popular and upcoming research fields in this domain to present new arenas with which further research would provide greater insights into the field of EPUs, thus proving relevant to the current world and proving beneficial to researchers as well as policymakers. Understanding the various areas impacted by EPUs can help policymakers prepare for uncertainty and formulate changes to hedge against difficulties. This work contributes significantly to advancing the area of EPUs by analyzing the field's knowledge structure to better understand existing and emerging issues. Introduction Economic policy uncertainty (EPU) is a construct that has drawn the attention of researchers and policymakers alike in recent years. (Berger et al., 2022; Dou et al., 2022; Su et al., 2021, Wang et al., 2022, Yu et al., 2021). The term "EPU" describes the unpredictability in the country, financial markets, investments, etc., as a result of unpredictability in government policymaking (Baker et al., 2016). Brogaard and Detzel (2015) define EPU as "the uncertainty regarding fiscal, regulatory, or monetary policy". EPU is also the inability to forecast the likelihood of the occurrence of an event against the associated risk. Uncertainty arises, affecting multiple aspects of an economy, when the path ahead for the government's policy decisions remains uncertain, or when it is unclear how different policy changes affect businesses. Policymakers must anticipate these uncertainties to mitigate negative economic impacts. Economic and political events are crucial in shaping a country’s growth trajectory. Periods of unrest and crisis typically reduce consumption, leading companies to adopt a conservative approach in investments, research and development, mergers, and acquisitions. EPU significantly affects business operations and national economic growth (Baker et al., 2016). In times of economic downturn, households and companies increase their precautionary savings, which further slows growth (Sharma & Khanna, 2023). For example, in China, depositors shift investments from time deposits to demand deposits, increasing liquidity risk, especially for smaller banks (Deng et al., 2023). Additionally, uncertainty drives capital away from countries because of concerns about information asymmetry and geopolitical instability. EPU impact has been studied across various sectors, including currency exchange rates (Abid, 2020), financial institutions (Caglayan & Xu, 2019), banks (Tran et al., 2021), stock returns (Arouri et al., 2016; Kang & Ratti, 2013), financial stability (Phan et al., 2021), Bitcoin (Demir et al., 2018), and investment (Wang et al., 2014; Kang et al., 2014). However, a comprehensive summary of the impact of EPU and its importance remains scarce, motivating this study. There is a need for a study examining the trend of research in this field and identifying future research directions. Given the importance of understanding the impact of the EPU on national and global economies, this study aims to provide retrospective research, offering insights for academics, managers, and policymakers. We employ bibliometric techniques to analyze large databases, which have gained popularity for exploring publication trends, evaluating journal Multidiscip. Rev. Data collection The data for this study were sourced from the Scopus database covering the period 2006--2022, as no relevant results were found during the search in the database before 2006. Research in the field only garnered attention after the formulation of the Baker index from Baker et al., 2016, as there was no quantifiable way to measure EPU before that. Bibliographic coupling Bibliographic coupling has gained importance and has been established as a revered technique for bibliometric analysis (Baker et al., 2021). Cocitation analysis employs the use of published citations and hence uses seminal knowledge. However, bibliographic coupling also encompasses works that have not received many citations and are therefore typically disregarded in cocitation studies. (Donthu et al., 2021). Bibliographic coupling is a technique that analyses the number of common references in two documents. If the reference list contains at least one commonly cited reference, the documents are said to be bibliographically coupled (Aria & Cuccurullo, 2017; Kessler, 1963). The greater the number of these shared references is, the greater the total link strength. The underlying presumption is that if two documents, sources and authors have similar references, they are examining the same theme. Limitations This study provides an overview of existing and emerging research in the field but has three main limitations. First, it relies on a single database that finds no research before 2006, potentially omitting earlier publications. To improve credibility, future studies may integrate additional databases such as Web of Science and Google Scholar. Second, certain types of works—such as theses, unpublished research, and working papers—were excluded, and the analysis focused only on publications in English. Expanding the scope to include these omissions could make the findings more globally relevant. Third, the analysis is limited to bibliometric techniques, which focus on citations but do not highlight an author's actual contribution or the context of their keywords. Supplementing these techniques with systematic literature reviews and meta- analyses could provide a deeper and more comprehensive understanding of the field. 6. Final Considerations This study evaluates economic policy uncertainty (EPU) from 2006--2022 via bibliometric analysis to identify trends, hot topics, and emerging themes. Tools such as cocitation analysis, bibliographic coupling, thematic analysis, alluvial maps, word clouds, and topic trends reveal popular and upcoming research areas. Two knowledge structures—intellectual and conceptual fields—are explored. The intellectual structure is analyzed through cocitation and bibliographic coupling of authors, sources, and references, clustering similar themes for a broad overview of EPU research. The conceptual structure employs thematic analysis, creating a thematic map based on centrality and density to highlight key topics. Thematic evolution from 2006--2021 and for 2022 is plotted, showcasing topic evolution and emerging themes. A roadmap of topic trends offers a concise view of the changing research focus. These tools uncover existing and new themes that, when further researched, could provide deeper insights into EPU. The study acknowledges its limitations, suggesting the inclusion of more databases and advanced techniques such as text mining for future research. By answering key questions and raising new ones, this study can aid policymakers in making informed decisions and identifying new research frontiers. Ethical Considerations Not applicable. JSON: Name: epu_multi_db_pipeline Title: A reproducible multi-database bibliometric and dynamic topic-modeling pipeline to map the intellectual and conceptual evolution of research on economic policy uncertainty Short Hypothesis: Integrating Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar bibliographic records and applying dynamic topic modeling to titles and abstracts will identify a significantly larger number of validated emerging economic policy uncertainty (EPU) themes than a Scopus-only cocitation/bibliographic-coupling analysis within the same time window. Related Work: Existing bibliometric studies of economic policy uncertainty typically use a single curated database (commonly Scopus), visualize citation networks with tools such as VOSviewer, and apply bibliographic coupling, cocitation analysis, and static thematic mapping (e.g., co-word analysis, bidimensional thematic maps). These studies provide reliable citation-based intellectual structure but suffer from limited coverage (omitting working papers, preprints and non-indexed outlets), language and database bias, and weak text-level semantic analysis. Prior work has not combined cross-database deduplication, normalized citation linking across sources, and recent neural text-embedding + dynamic topic models to jointly analyze citation structure and evolving semantic themes. Limitations in current methods include dependence on citation counts (which lag and bias toward older works), coarse temporal slicing, limited reproducibility for merged data, and weak validation of automatically detected 'emerging' themes against external evidence or expert labels. Abstract: Problem: Single-database bibliometric analyses risk missing publications and emerging themes in the rapidly growing economic policy uncertainty (EPU) literature. Approach: We propose a reproducible pipeline that (1) harvests records from Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar for a common keyword set, (2) performs metadata normalization and DOI-based deduplication, (3) constructs citation and bibliographic-coupling networks, and (4) applies dynamic neural topic modeling (sentence embeddings + time-aware clustering) on titles/abstracts to detect evolving conceptual themes. Contribution: The pipeline integrates citation-based and text-based analyses, provides ablation comparisons to Scopus-only and citation-only baselines, and outputs validated time-ordered theme trajectories. Expected outcome: Empirical evaluation will demonstrate higher recall of relevant items, improved detection of short-lived and nascent themes, and greater temporal resolution of thematic shifts in EPU research, enabling more accurate mapping for researchers and policymakers. The pipeline and evaluation are provided as reproducible code and data artifacts. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Scopus export of records (title, abstract, authors, affiliations, venue, DOI, citations) for keyword query "economic policy uncertainty" OR "EPU" for years 2006--2024; (2) Web of Science (WoS) export for same query and date window; (3) Google Scholar harvest via Publish or Perish for same query and window; (4) SSRN and RePEc metadata (optional). Inclusion criteria: English-language records plus Chinese-English bilingual subset for sensitivity; record types: articles, reviews, conference papers, preprints/working papers (where available). Preprocessing: DOI- and title-fingerprint deduplication; normalize venue names; unify citation links by DOI or canonicalized title; remove records without abstract. Proposed pipeline (P): combined dataset + citation network construction + dynamic topic modeling. Baselines: B1 = Scopus-only replication using cocitation + bibliographic coupling (VOSviewer-style); B2 = combined-dataset citation analysis without text modeling; B3 = combined-dataset + classical LDA static topic modeling. Text pipeline configuration: embedding model = sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2; dimensionality reduction UMAP (n_neighbors=15, n_components=5, min_dist=0.1); clustering = HDBSCAN (min_cluster_size=15, min_samples=5); dynamic modeling = run per rolling 3-year windows and apply topic alignment by Jaccard-overlap of top-n words and cluster centroid cosine similarity; tune hyperparameters by grid search. Evaluation metrics: (a) recall of a curated ground truth list of seminal EPU works (coverage of citations across datasets); (b) additional-theme yield = count of distinct validated themes detected by P that are absent in B1; (c) thematic coherence (CV coherence) and topic stability (mean pairwise centroid cosine over adjacent windows); (d) cluster agreement with expert labels (precision, recall, F1); (e) network coverage: fraction of citation edges present relative to union graph; (f) statistical tests: McNemar test for paired theme-detection differences and bootstrap CIs. Experimental setup: run P and baselines on same hardware (single-node with 64GB RAM, 16 vCPUs); fix random seed for embedding and clustering; time-slicing: yearly and 3-year rolling; perform ablation studies: (A1) remove Google Scholar records; (A2) remove text-embedding (use title-only); (A3) replace HDBSCAN+embeddings with LDA (k=30). Reporting: number of records ingested, deduplicated set size, runtime, memory; top 20 topics per year with top 10 terms and representative documents; quantitative comparisons across metrics and ablations with p-values. Risk Factors and Limitations: Coverage bias across data sources (incomplete or inconsistent indexing between Scopus, WoS and Google Scholar) leading to non-random omissions; DOI and metadata mismatches causing false duplicates or failed linkage of citations; language bias if non-English abstracts unavailable; Google Scholar scraping/legal/consistency issues and variable metadata quality; citation-count lag and disciplinary citation practices biasing network centrality measures; embedding and clustering sensitivity to hyperparameters leading to unstable topic assignments; computational costs and memory constraints for embedding and clustering large corpora (tens of thousands of records) on modest hardware; inability of unsupervised topic models to provide semantically precise labels (requires expert validation); temporal alignment challenges when topics split or merge rapidly, producing ambiguous theme trajectories; results may not generalize to other research domains with different publication or citation dynamics.
